assistant:
**Answer: you don't need an optimization model or an AI tool.**
**Why:** you already serve every registered household that comes, in 49 of 52 weeks, so there's no choice about who gets food for a model to improve. What's left is keeping enough boxes on hand, and a simple counting rule handles that.
**Next steps this month:** (1) Add up last year's sign-in sheets, week by week. (2) Set a buffer of extra boxes and a written plan for short weeks. (3) Talk to the foundation about putting the grant toward stock, storage or dietary options instead of software.

## 1. What kind of problem this is

None of the twelve allocation types fits, and that's good news. A model helps when you have to choose who gets something scarce, when needs change in ways you can't see, or when you don't know which option works. You described none of these. Every household that comes gets a box, there's one kind of box, supply has met demand 49 weeks out of 52, and the shortfalls were small (10–20 boxes out of about 150).

Your two real questions are practical, not mathematical:
- **How many boxes to have ready**, especially at the end of the month.
- **How to offer halal and vegetarian boxes** without running out of either.

This is the taxonomy's own example of "no model needed": an AI system to set pantry quantities when every household already gets served.

## 2. What goes wrong with an AI tool here

- **It can't learn much.** A model trained on 52 weeks of tick marks, with only three short weeks, would know barely more than a volunteer with a calculator.
- **Nobody keeps it running.** The shift lead changes every few months, and you have one laptop. Tools that depend on one person usually stop working when that person leaves.
- **It adds data entry and privacy risk.** Typing names, family details and dietary needs into a system makes a record of people's religion (halal) and circumstances, all to answer a question you can answer with totals.
- **It could make things less fair.** Many "fair allocation" tools score or rank households. Once a pantry has scores, it's tempting to give less to people scored as "lower need". Today everyone who comes gets a box, which is about as fair as it gets.

What goes wrong with *no plan* is a short week now and then. A buffer and a short-week rule fix that.

## 3. How it runs on the ground

**A weekly tally sheet (paper, one page).** At closing, the shift lead fills in one line:

| Week | Date | Boxes ready | Households served | Standard / Halal / Veg | Ran out? (time) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

Write totals only, never names. Add a column to the sign-in sheet where households tick H or V, so the counts are easy.

**A packing rule posted on the wall:**
- **Normal weeks:** pack the highest number served in the last four weeks, plus 15 extra. The buffer matches your shortfalls of 10–20 boxes; adjust it after checking the sheets.
- **Last week of the month:** use the highest count from recent end-of-month weeks, plus 15.
- **Halal and vegetarian:** pack the highest count of each from the last four weeks, plus 3 [to check: adjust once you see your real numbers].

**A short-week plan, decided ahead of time:**
- Keep shelf-stable reserve boxes (rice, beans, canned goods), including halal and vegetarian ones.
- If those run out too, have a referral card or voucher for a partner pantry, or offer pickup the next day.
- Agree in advance whether, in a short week, the last hour gets slightly smaller boxes so everyone gets something. Write the rule down, so whoever is shift lead doesn't have to decide on the spot.

**On the laptop, optional:** a single spreadsheet tab where someone types in the weekly totals each month, with a chart. That takes about ten minutes a month, and any volunteer can do it.

## 4. Where it has been used

Most pantries plan this way already: counts and a buffer, run by hand. I know of no documented case of a model improving a pantry of your size. Optimization does work for food further up the supply chain, where there are many sites and much larger volumes:
- **Feeding America's "Choice System"** lets food banks bid for donated truckloads as they arrive, using an internal credit currency (Prendergast, *Journal of Political Economy*, 2022). It solves a problem *between* food banks, not inside a pantry.
- **WFP's Optimus** designs food baskets and sourcing across whole national operations. In Iraq it cut costs by 12% at the same nutritional value (Peters et al., 2021).

Both show where models earn their keep: hundreds of sites, many decisions, and analysts to run them. Neither describes your situation. Check the primary sources before quoting these anywhere.

## 5. What worked and what was hard

**What works:** simple, written rules that survive volunteer turnover. Your 49-of-52 record shows the current approach mostly works already.

**What's hard:** keeping the habit going when shift leads change. Put the tally sheet and rules in a binder at the sign-in table, and make filling in the tally part of closing up.

**Blind spots in your records:**
- **Who doesn't come.** Sign-in sheets count who showed up, not registered households who stopped coming or can't make it during open hours. That may be where the fairness problem really is. Compare the number of registered households with the number served each week.
- **Why the three short weeks happened.** Did less food arrive, or did more people come? The answer changes the fix: more supply, or a bigger buffer.
- **Late arrivals.** If people who come later get fewer choices (no halal boxes left, for example), that's unfair in a way the totals won't show. Note the time you run out of each type.

**Ethics:** keep dietary and religious information to tick marks and totals, store the sheets securely, and never use them to decide who gets less.

## 6. The simpler option

The plan above *is* the simpler option. Compared with any model:
- **Total:** very close, since supply already covers nearly every week.
- **Fairness:** at least as good, because everyone who comes is served and nobody is scored or ranked.
- **Worst case:** better than a forecast, since a buffer and reserve boxes cover surprises a model would miss.
- **Evidence:** the weekly tally gives you clear numbers to show the foundation.

What it gives up: almost nothing at your size. It won't predict a sudden jump in demand, but neither would a model trained on a year of paper sheets.

**Check before settling on it:**
- Demand is fairly steady, and the three short weeks weren't the start of a trend.
- The registered list reflects real need, and eligible households aren't being turned away or put off by your hours.
- The halal and vegetarian counts stay fairly stable.

**How to test it on past records:** go through last year's 52 sheets and ask whether the buffer rule would have covered the three short weeks, and how many extra boxes it would have packed in total (your cost in food and possible spoilage). That one afternoon is the whole test.

**When to look again:** if you run short more than three or four times a year, if a waitlist forms, if registrations grow well beyond 150, or if supply becomes regularly too small for demand. Even then, the next step would be a published rationing rule (for example, a fixed share per household), not an AI tool.

**About the grant:** "fairer" could mean shelf-stable reserve stock, halal and vegetarian supplies, storage space, extra pickup hours for households who can't come now, or a few hours of volunteer time to set up the tally system. Any of these would probably do more for fairness than software.

---

**Follow-ups, one at a time if you'd like:**
1. Fit the plan to your pantry
2. Readiness checks
3. Pilot design (testing the buffer rule)
4. Build options: tools and partners
5. Reading and people to contact
6. One-page brief for the foundation, explaining what you'd fund instead
